text: Every request to the Orbit API must carry an API key in the X-Orbit-Key header. Keys are created in the dashboard under Settings, and each key belongs to exactly one workspace. A key is shown once at creation and cannot be retrieved later.

To replace a credential without downtime, create a second key, deploy it, then revoke the old one. Orbit accepts both during the overlap. Revocation takes effect within sixty seconds across all regions.

Keys can be restricted to read-only access or to a single resource type. A request made with insufficient permission returns error E4031. Scopes are fixed when the key is created and cannot be edited afterwards.

Each workspace may send 600 requests per minute. When the limit is exceeded the API responds with HTTP 429 and error E4291. The Retry-After header tells the client how many seconds to wait before trying again.

Short spikes are tolerated: a workspace can exceed its steady allowance by up to 100 extra calls in any ten second window. Sustained traffic above the allowance is throttled regardless of this burst allowance.

List endpoints return at most 50 items per page. The response includes a next_cursor field; pass it back as the cursor query parameter to fetch the following page. When next_cursor is null there are no more results.

To make a write safe to retry, send an Idempotency-Key header with a unique value. If the same key is seen again within 24 hours, Orbit returns the original response instead of performing the operation twice.

Orbit can notify your server when something changes. Register an HTTPS endpoint in the dashboard and choose which event types to receive. Each delivery is a POST request with a JSON body describing the event.

Every webhook delivery includes an X-Orbit-Signature header containing an HMAC-SHA256 of the raw body, computed with your endpoint secret. Reject any delivery whose signature does not match, and compare using a constant-time function.

If your endpoint does not answer with a 2xx status within ten seconds, the delivery is attempted again with exponential backoff for up to three days. After the final failed attempt the endpoint is disabled and the workspace owner is emailed.

Failed requests return a JSON object with three fields: code, message and request_id. The code is stable and safe to branch on; the message is written for humans and may change. Quote the request_id when contacting support.

A request with a missing or malformed field returns HTTP 422 and error E4220. The response lists every invalid field in an errors array, so a form can show all problems at once instead of one at a time.
Error E5000 means something went wrong on Orbit's side. These requests are safe to retry with backoff. If E5000 persists for more than a few minutes, check the status page before opening a ticket.
The API closes any connection that has not completed within 30 seconds and returns error E5040. Long-running work should be started as a job and polled, rather than held open on a single request.

Operations that take longer than a few seconds run as background jobs. Starting one returns a job id immediately. Poll the job endpoint until its state is succeeded or failed, or subscribe to the job.finished event instead of polling.
Files up to 5 GB are uploaded in parts. Request an upload session, send each part of at most 64 MB to the returned URLs, then complete the session. Parts may be sent in parallel and in any order.
An interrupted transfer does not have to start over. Ask the session which parts it already holds and send only the missing ones. Unfinished sessions are discarded after seven days.

Data is stored in the region chosen when the workspace is created: us-east, eu-west or ap-south. The region cannot be changed later. Requests are routed automatically, but latency is lowest when calling from the same continent.
Deleted records are kept in a recoverable state for 30 days and then erased permanently. Audit logs are retained for one year. Workspaces on the enterprise plan can shorten or lengthen both periods.

A full copy of a workspace's records can be requested from the dashboard. The archive is prepared as a background job and delivered as newline-delimited JSON, one file per resource type, available for download for 48 hours.

The official Python client is installed with pip install orbit-sdk. It reads the key from the ORBIT_API_KEY environment variable, retries idempotent calls automatically, and exposes every list endpoint as an iterator that follows cursors for you.
The JavaScript client supports Node 20 and later. Pass the key to the constructor or set ORBIT_API_KEY. All methods return promises, and list methods are async iterators.
The API is versioned by date. Send the Orbit-Version header, for example 2026-03-01, to pin behaviour. Requests without the header use the version that was current when the workspace was created.

A version is supported for at least 18 months after its successor ships. Responses from a version scheduled for removal carry a Sunset header with the shutdown date, and workspace owners are emailed 90 days ahead.

Every workspace has a test mode with separate keys beginning sk_test_. Nothing done in test mode touches live data or sends real notifications, and its contents can be wiped from the dashboard at any time.

Records can be queried with a filter expression, for example status:active AND created>2026-01-01. Results are eventually consistent: a record may take up to two seconds to appear in search after it is written.

Up to 500 writes can be combined into one batch request. Each item succeeds or fails independently, and the response reports a result per item in the same order. A batch counts as one request against the rate limit.
Team members can sign in to the dashboard through a company identity provider using SAML 2.0. Once single sign-on is enforced, password login is disabled for everyone except the workspace owner.
Usage is charged monthly by the number of stored records and the number of API calls. Invoices are issued on the first day of the month, and a workspace is suspended if a payment is 14 days overdue.
Current uptime and incident history are published at status.orbit.example. You can subscribe there to be alerted by email or webhook whenever an incident is opened, updated or resolved.
